extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, policymakers, and citizens interested in public opinion, public policy, and social reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying general criteria for judging public opinions, arguments, and social-political reasoning—focusing on stereotyping, spatial/temporal perspective, sampling, causation, and emotion-driven error. Useful for evaluating public discourse, policy arguments, and popular claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of false absolutism of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for arguments framed as 'eternal principles' or absolutist stereotypes that 'censor out all the objections, isolate the issue from its background and its context' and set off strong, inappropriate emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such framing turns discussion into fighting: once begun it requires invoking more absolute principles to defend what is attacked, then defenses for the defenses, etc. Be alert to rhetoric that substitutes a principle for engagement with concrete facts (anti-pattern: arguing from 'factless' principles about factories, mines, mountains, or political authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contradiction as a diagnostic clue of constructed stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of contradictions in an argument often shows how the argument was constructed and that the stereotype is being used to obliterate interfering facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you detect internal contradictions that seem to prop up a single claim, treat this as evidence the claim is stereotyping or ideologically constructed (example: the Ruritanian propaganda where principles 'blanketed each other' and contradictions revealed the construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for space (practical geography) in reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reasoning that ignores physical distances, transportation, and other practical geographical constraints—'inability to take account of space' is a common clue to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims by asking about real-world logistics: what transportation exists, how fast it moves, costs, routes, seasonal conditions, and detours. Anti-patterns include projecting forces or policies across thousands of miles without considering intervening terrain or infrastructure (example: imagining Japanese troops transported from Vladivostok to Poland as if 'on a magic carpet').

rubrics_metrics.name: Design boundaries and policies with practical geography in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing frontiers or making territorial/policy decisions, consider how lines operate on the ground—ethnic or colored maps that look 'just' may run through factories, streets, churches, or separate pasture from water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether abstract lines will create absurd complications in real use; prefer solutions that respect functional geography (railheads, water sources, market access) rather than only ethno-historical abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time and adopt the appropriate time-conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Time, like space, is often misconceived: decision-makers must choose the proper temporal horizon (emergency, season, decade, century) appropriate to the issue rather than applying a single 'Here and Now' perspective to all problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a decision requires short-term emergency calculation or long-run planning. Examples: wills and the law against perpetuities, constitution amending clauses, and recognizing that different time scales (geological, biological, social) demand different judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a realistic temporal horizon for posterity and restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: When policy affects future generations (forestry, coal reserves, long-term contracts), explicitly decide what you mean by 'posterity' and choose a realistic timescale for restoration, discovery of alternatives, or compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute available reserves, rates of use, feasible economies, and then square that computation with an explicit ideal standard for how far into the future obligations run (example: forestry replanting schedules; coal resource management; avoidance of 99-year monopolies that may lock future generations into inferior technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jumping necessary steps in sequences when imagining the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of proposals that assume immediate readiness for complex responsibilities (e.g., sudden imposition of industrial management roles without training) or that deny the time needed for development of capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs where assumption of responsibility proceeds in parallel with training and development; treat abrupt revolutionary shortcuts and simplistic rotations-in-office as symptoms of a mistaken time-conception (anti-pattern: assuming experts or wisdom can appear fully formed without preparation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper sampling methods; beware of selection bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations about large classes require carefully selected, representative samples; casual selection methods (asking accessible or affiliated groups) produce 'entirely worthless results.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statistical advice: use neutral, accidental, or random methods of approach; compute required sample sizes (example: Bowley's advice for Sheffield: 408 men and 408 women for a fair sample). Avoid sampling through philanthropic contacts, clubs, missions, or other nonrandom access points that bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat convenient or small samples as representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Casual impressions or the first few agreeing people are not reliable evidence of general truth; the presumption is against true representativeness when acting on casual impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the human tendency to 'spread a little butter over the whole universe'—corroborate impressions with systematic sampling or acknowledge uncertainty. Examples: employers judging all labor by most troublesome or most docile employees; radicals mistaking their group for the whole working class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective historical argumentation (pick your start date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from history commonly select dates or episodes that support one's position (e.g., Alsace-Lorraine belongs to whoever picks the favorable epoch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using historical claims, make explicit the temporal starting point and be alert to how different starting points produce different 'truths'; avoid presenting selective history as objective justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the faith-ladder: do not convert desired ends into present truths
rubrics_metrics.description: William James's 'faith ladder' shows how belief can escalate from possibility to certainty ('it shall be true, at any rate true for me'), leading people to project desired futures back into present fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist substituting goals for starting points; avoid reading into the present the conditions that courage, effort, and skill might create in the future. Treat hopeful instances as evidence, not proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty causal inference and post hoc ergo propter hoc reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Untrained minds readily infer causation from sequence or simultaneity (post hoc) or from emotionally-linked events; emotion leads us to collect co-feeling items into causal systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand disciplined causal investigation for complicated social phenomena; beware of attributing complex outcomes to single causes because they appear together (examples: smallpox blamed on alehouses; Relativity tied to Bolshevism). Check for confounders, parallel trends, and seek scholarly analysis rather than intuitive leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize emotion-driven associative entanglement as a source of systematic error
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong feelings attach disparate ideas and memories into a tangled causal narrative—'anything can be related to anything else, provided it feels like it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering sweeping 'systems of all evil' (or all good), examine how emotion may have welded otherwise unrelated facts into a single explanation; separate affective resonance from logical or evidentiary linkage.
